title: Manjrekar Calls Out BCCI and ICC Over Lenient Penalties for Jaiswal and Sooryavanshi
excerpt: The former India batter argues that light fines for physical altercations ‘train players to repeat’ aggressive behavior and risk their careers.
body:
• Sanjay Manjrekar criticized the BCCI and ICC for insufficient penalties after Yashasvi Jaiswal’s physical confrontation with Sri Lanka’s Asitha Fernando during the second Test in Colombo
  • Jaiswal and Fernando each received a 25% match fee fine and one demerit point for the helmet-to-forehead altercation on August 23
  • Manjrekar linked the incident to teenager Vaibhav Sooryavanshi’s earlier physical altercation during the India A tri-series against Sri Lanka, arguing both cases show a pattern of leniency

Former India batter Sanjay Manjrekar has sharply criticized the International Cricket Council and the Board of Control for Cricket in India for what he sees as inadequate punishment of on-field physical altercations involving Indian players.

The criticism, posted on X on Wednesday, followed the ICC’s decision to fine India opener Yashasvi Jaiswal and Sri Lanka fast bowler Asitha Fernando 25% of their match fees and hand each one demerit point after a heated confrontation during the ongoing second Test in Colombo.

What Happened on the Field

The incident occurred on the first day of the second Test at the Sinhalese Sports Club ground on August 23. Fernando dismissed Jaiswal after the opener had hit three boundaries in the over. As Jaiswal walked back toward the pavilion, he turned and approached Fernando. The two players came face to face, with Jaiswal’s helmet making contact with Fernando’s forehead, before teammates intervened to separate them.

Both players admitted to breaching Article 2.12 of the ICC Code of Conduct, which covers inappropriate physical contact, and accepted the sanctions proposed by match referee Andy Pycroft.

A Pattern of Leniency, Manjrekar Argues

Manjrekar drew a direct line between the Jaiswal episode and an earlier incident involving 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi during India A’s tri-nation series in Sri Lanka in June. After a tense Super Over loss to Sri Lanka A in Dambulla, Sooryavanshi confronted and pushed opposition player Vishen Halambage. Both players were fined 50% of their match fees, with India A captain Tilak Varma also penalized 30%.

“Dear ICC and BCCI — Vaibhav for India A recently and now Jaiswal. If you keep letting them get away with such behaviour, you train them to repeat such behaviour. It’s not good for the sport and crucially their own future too.”

— Sanjay Manjrekar, on X, August 26, 2026

Manjrekar’s argument centers on deterrence: financial penalties and demerit points, he contends, are insufficient to discourage young players from crossing the line. He has been consistent on this stance — after Sooryavanshi’s June incident, he wrote that he would have dropped the teenager from the next India A match to send a clear message.

Fan Pushback and the Broader Debate

Not everyone agrees with Manjrekar’s assessment. Several fans pointed out on social media that Jaiswal did not “get away” with the incident — he was formally charged, admitted the offense, and accepted the sanction. Others noted that Fernando was equally involved and received identical punishment.

The debate reflects a broader tension in cricket between protecting the sport’s traditions of sportsmanship and the aggressive, emotion-fueled intensity that modern players bring to Test cricket. The ICC’s demerit-point system triggers escalating consequences — four points within 24 months result in a match suspension — but critics argue that threshold is too distant to influence behavior in the heat of the moment.

India’s two-Test series against Sri Lanka continues, with the second Test in Colombo still in progress. Jaiswal, who scored a century in the first Test at Galle, remains one of India’s most explosive young batters at age 24.
